trivia_fact: Linus Torvalds originally called his project "Freax" (free + freak + Unix). Ari Lemmke, the FTP server admin at Helsinki University, rejected that name and listed it as "linux" instead. Linus considered the name "Linux" too egotistical but eventually accepted it.

In 1992, Andrew Tanenbaum (MINIX creator) publicly declared Linux "obsolete" because it used a monolithic kernel instead of a microkernel design. Torvalds responded that practical performance mattered more than theoretical purity. The debate is now studied in OS courses as a case study in engineering trade-offs.

Linus Torvalds chose a penguin because he was reportedly bitten by a little penguin at the Canberra Zoo in Australia and developed "penguinitis" — a fondness for penguins. Larry Ewing created the Tux image in 1996 using GIMP. The name "Tux" may derive from "Torvalds' Unix."

Kernel panic dates back to Unix V5 at Bell Labs (1974). The panic() function was called when the kernel encountered an unrecoverable error. The term was deliberately dramatic — if the kernel itself panics, the situation is truly dire. Linux inherited this terminology directly.

The Unix epoch (time zero) is January 1, 1970, 00:00:00 UTC because that was roughly when Unix was being developed at Bell Labs. It was a round, recent date that minimized wasted bits. The original time_t was a 32-bit integer counting seconds, giving a range until January 19, 2038.

/etc originally meant "et cetera" — it was a dumping ground for files that didn't fit elsewhere in early Unix. The backronym "Editable Text Configuration" emerged later but was never official. Dennis Ritchie confirmed it was simply the catch-all directory.

Root is UID 0 because the kernel checks for UID 0 specifically when determining superuser privileges — it's hardcoded, not configurable. This means you could rename the "root" account to anything and it would still be the superuser. The name "root" refers to the root of the filesystem (/).

On January 19, 2038, at 03:14:07 UTC, 32-bit signed time_t values will overflow, wrapping to December 13, 1901. Linux addressed this by moving to 64-bit time_t (good until the year 292,277,026,596). Embedded systems and legacy 32-bit code remain vulnerable.

Linux uses a monolithic kernel (all drivers in kernel space) not because Torvalds believed it was theoretically superior, but because it was simpler to implement and faster. Loadable kernel modules (added later) gave Linux some of the flexibility of microkernels while keeping performance.

Daemon in computing comes from Maxwell's demon, a thought experiment in physics about an entity that works in the background sorting molecules. The usage was adopted at MIT's Project MAC in the 1960s. Daemons are not "demons" — the spelling distinction is intentional.

PID 1 (init/systemd) has unique kernel protections: signals without an explicit handler are silently dropped (even SIGKILL in some contexts), it adopts orphaned processes, and if PID 1 dies, the kernel panics immediately. No other process has these properties.

The "everything is a file" philosophy originated with Unix at Bell Labs. Dennis Ritchie and Ken Thompson realized that using the same read/write/open/close interface for devices, pipes, sockets, and files made programs composable. This is why you can `cat /proc/cpuinfo` — even process info is a "file."

POSIX (Portable Operating System Interface) was proposed by Richard Stallman when IEEE asked for a name for their Unix standardization effort. He suggested adding "X" to make it sound like Unix. The standard resolved the "Unix wars" between AT&T System V and BSD, giving developers a common target.

GNU stands for "GNU's Not Unix" — a recursive acronym, a hacker tradition where the definition references itself. Richard Stallman started the GNU Project in 1983 to create a complete free Unix-like OS. Linux became the kernel that completed the GNU system, leading to the "GNU/Linux" naming debate.

Linus Torvalds announced Linux on comp.os.minix on August 25, 1991, writing: "I'm doing a (free) operating system (just a hobby, won't be big and professional like gnu)." This may be the most spectacularly wrong self-assessment in computing history.

The first Linux distributions appeared in 1992. MCC Interim Linux and TAMU were among the earliest. Slackware (1993) and Debian (1993) are the oldest still-active distributions. Most modern distros descend from either Debian (Ubuntu, Mint) or Red Hat (Fedora, CentOS).

Linux 1.0 (1994) had about 176,000 lines of code. By version 6.x (2023), it exceeded 30 million lines. Over 15,000 developers from 1,500+ companies have contributed. The kernel receives roughly 80,000 commits per year — about 9 commits per hour.

Unix began in 1969 when Ken Thompson wrote it on a PDP-7 he found in a corner at Bell Labs. He wrote the first version in three weeks — one week each for the OS, the shell, and the editor. Thompson and Dennis Ritchie then rewrote Unix in C (1973), making it the first portable OS.

The AT&T vs. BSD lawsuit (1992-1994) created legal uncertainty around BSD Unix at precisely the time Linux emerged. If BSD had been unencumbered, Linux might never have gained traction. By the time BSD was cleared, Linux had built an unstoppable community.

Since November 2017, 100% of the world's top 500 supercomputers run Linux. The last non-Linux entry was a Chinese system running AIX. Linux dominates because it can be customized for extreme-scale workloads in ways proprietary OSes cannot.

Linus chose the GPLv2 license not for ideological reasons but as a "tit-for-tat" strategy: if you use my code, share your improvements. He has publicly refused to adopt GPLv3, calling some of its provisions "evil." The kernel is permanently GPLv2-only — it would require agreement from thousands of contributors to change.

The /usr directory does not stand for "user." In early Unix, /usr was a second disk partition where user home directories lived (the first disk held /bin and /etc). When a third disk was added for actual user homes (/home), /usr kept its name but became the system programs directory.

Android uses the Linux kernel — every Android phone runs Linux. Google maintains its own kernel branch with mobile-specific patches. This makes Linux by far the most-used OS kernel in the world, powering billions of phones, servers, embedded devices, and supercomputers simultaneously.

Some Linux servers have run for over 10 years without rebooting, though this is no longer recommended (security patches require reboots). Livepatch technology (since kernel 4.0, 2015) allows applying kernel security fixes without rebooting, reducing the need for such extreme uptimes.

Over 75% of Linux kernel development is done by paid corporate developers. The top contributors include Intel, Red Hat, Google, AMD, and Meta. Despite the "hobbyist" origin story, Linux kernel development is now one of the most professionally managed open-source projects in the world.
